results.summary: Cirrhotic patients with concurrent advanced malignancy who develop HE represent a high-risk group. MELD score and cancer stage are independent predictors. However, HE episodes precipitated by reversible factors (mild hyperammonemia, drug effects) can respond to treatment even in advanced disease. Goals of care discussions should include prognosis from both liver disease and malignancy.

differential.key_features: Enzalutamide crosses BBB and causes fatigue, cognitive decline, rare seizures; consider dose modification with oncology if HE management does not fully restore cognition.
MRI brain with gadolinium required to exclude; rare in prostate but possible; CSF if MRI suspicious.
Leuprolide-induced testosterone suppression contributes to cognitive/fatigue symptoms but not asterixis.
Insidious onset in 60s could fit; lactulose response distinguishes.
Check Ca; prostate metastases can cause hypercalcemia.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.

Targeted oncologic agents (enzalutamide, abiraterone, BTK inhibitors) can cross the BBB and produce neuropsychiatric symptoms — always entertain when a cancer patient on these drugs presents with confusion.
Even mild ammonia elevation in a cirrhotic with insidious cognitive decline can represent covert HE; a lactulose trial is informative.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MRI with gadolinium is appropriate to exclude leptomeningeal disease, but the dominant treatable cause is HE; do not delay lactulose trial waiting for MRI.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C. is a 61-year-old man with NASH cirrhosis and castration-resistant prostate cancer on enzalutamide who presents with 3 weeks of slowly progressive confusion, emotional blunting, and passivity. His wife noticed he was no longer engaged in conversation, was having difficulty following complex discussions, and seemed 'far away.' He had a prior grade 1 HE episode 4 months ago that resolved with rifaximin. His ammonia on admission is 64 µmol/L — only mildly elevated. His EEG shows non-specific slowing. His CT head is negative for metastatic disease.

neurological_exam.additional: No jaundice. Mild ascites on exam. Spiders absent. PSA elevated (known prostate cancer). CT head shows no evidence of prostate cancer brain metastasis. Wife notes he is passively apathetic — 'not himself' for 3 weeks.

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Oriented to person and place; disoriented to time. Slow processing. Mild asterixis. Wife notes behavioral change including passivity and emotional blunting over 3 weeks — possibly new vs prior episode. No asterixis at home observation.
